newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Rwandan refugees end Zaire trek in warring Congo.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees end Zaire trek in warring Congo.

text.p: For some 150 Rwandan Hutu refugees a day, a nightmare trek across the former Zaire, Africa's third largest country, ends with a short canoe trip to safety in the "other" Congo.

But just when they thought the misery was over, the ill-fated refugees find the spectre of war hovering over their new haven with rival factions, largely ethnically based, clashing in the capital Brazzaville.

The fighting has not spread beyond the capital, where a truce was in force on Saturday. It has disrupted aid supplies to camps along the Congo river that divides the Congo Republic from the Democratic Republic of Congo, ex-Zaire.
The survivors of an up to 3,000 km (2,000 miles) trek through the forest, jungle and swamp of what is now Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo are the fit or the lucky.

"The forest in ex-Zaire has been a killing obstacle at times so you see here mainly men in good shape with few health problems," Paul Stromberg, of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, said at Lukolela, a camp by the river holding 6,000 people.
"We see more and more people who left their children behind because they were unable to feed them in the jungle."
Kabila, whose forces toppled dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May, said on Friday there were no more Rwandan refugees in his country. The exodus across the river tells a different story.
Around 150 Rwandan Hutu refugees cross by canoe each day saying they fear former Zaire's new rulers are out to kill them. Congo-Brazzaville, even at war, is a safer bet.
Among them are armed Hutu militia who took part in the 1994 genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis in Rwanda.
A Tutsi army overran their homeland despite the slaughter, and some two million Hutus, the innocent along with the guilty, fled to neighbouring countries, mostly to Zaire.
Kabila's Tutsi-based rebellion last year sent them fleeing their U.N. camps in east Zaire which the Hutu militias, still armed, had effectively controlled.
Some 800,000 went home reluctantly but tens of thousands more fled west through the country with the rebels in pursuit.
There are persistent allegations that thousands were massacred by Kabila's forces or by allies from Rwanda or Uganda, his allies. A U.N. team arrived on Friday to investigate.
Alfonse, a student who fled Rwanda after the genocide three years ago, said he had moved from one squalid camp to the next.

The Hutu militiamen among the refugees, whose cross-border attacks on Rwanda helped ignite the Zaire crisis, are finally handing in their weapons in Congo. "They are voluntarily laying down their arms because they no longer feel threatened. There are few tensions here," Stromberg said.

They make up about six percent of the 6,000 refugees at Lukolela. A grass-hut camp, it sits by a small village beside the fast-flowing, mud-coloured Congo River and is 300 km (200 miles) north of Brazzaville and one degree south of the equator.
The crossing is very orderly. Newcomers hire a canoe to take them out to an island in the river. There a motorised canoe picks them up, 40 at a time, and takes them to the other side.
They are registered, disarmed of knives, machetes or guns, fed on beans, rice and maize and given medical treatment, usually for sores and feet swollen by their great trek.
Eighty percent of them are men and some end up working for the locals to supplement their rations with fish.
Stromberg said some wanted to go home to Rwanda. "We're at a loss as to what to do with those who want to stay," he added.
